question: I teach a class with 30 students. I want to keep their gradebook in my personal Google Drive so I can access it from home. Is that OK under Duke's data policy?
reference: No. Student grade data is classified as Sensitive under Duke's Data Classification Policy (oit.duke.edu/security/data-classification). Personal Google Drive accounts (not Duke-managed Workspace) are not approved for Sensitive data — Duke does not hold a Business Associate Agreement or Data Use Agreement covering personal accounts. Use one of the Duke-approved options: Duke Box (box.duke.edu), Duke Google Workspace for Education (your @duke.edu account, not a personal Gmail), or your course's learning management system (Canvas) which is purpose-built for grade data. To access from home, log into the Duke VPN or use the web interface of an approved tool. For questions, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I want to use ChatGPT to help me draft feedback comments on student essays. Can I paste in the essay content and the student's name?
reference: No, not the public consumer ChatGPT website. The public chat.openai.com is NOT covered by a Duke data use agreement and should not receive any student-identifying information, student work, grades, or any data classified as Sensitive or Restricted under Duke's Data Classification Policy. Student essays plus identifying details are Sensitive under FERPA. The approved alternative is Duke's AI Gateway (Duke GPT or other Duke-hosted models accessed via litellm.oit.duke.edu) when used for purposes the data classification policy allows; even there, double-check whether the specific use case is permitted before pasting student data. If you only need help with feedback PHRASING, anonymize the content first (remove names, identifying details) before sending it to any AI tool. For questions on what data is appropriate for each tool, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: As a TA, can I store scanned copies of student exams in Duke Box if I keep the folder private?
reference: Yes, with conditions. Duke Box (box.duke.edu) is licensed by Duke and is an approved tool for Sensitive data including student work, so scanned exams with student identifying information can be stored there. Two policy conditions to follow: (1) Sharing — keep the folder private to you (or share only with other Duke staff who have a legitimate educational need under FERPA); do NOT share with external collaborators or with student personal email addresses. Box's default share link settings can be more permissive than you intend, so review them. (2) Retention — follow your department's record retention policy; exam materials are typically retained for one academic term plus the appeals window, then deleted. Do not store exams indefinitely. For data classification questions, see oit.duke.edu/security/data-classification or contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I just received an email from someone claiming to be 'Duke IT Support' asking me to click a link to reset my NetID password because of a security incident. The email looks somewhat legitimate but I'm not sure. What should I do?
reference: Treat it as a likely phishing attempt and do NOT click the link. Duke OIT does not request password resets via unsolicited email; password resets go through the NetID self-service portal at oit.duke.edu, never through a link in an inbound email. Three steps: (1) Do not click the link, do not enter your NetID password anywhere prompted by that email, do not download any attachment. (2) Report the suspected phishing message to Duke IT Security — forward it as an attachment to abuse@duke.edu (or use the Outlook 'Report Phishing' button if you are on Duke email). (3) If you already clicked the link or entered your credentials, change your NetID password immediately at oit.duke.edu, then call the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200 to report the potential compromise so they can review account activity. Do not approve any unexpected Duo prompts in the meantime — those would also indicate someone is using your stolen credentials.
